subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the few remarks that I shall make in connection with this debate will be directed towards certain statements that have been made and certain opinions that have been expressed with which I may presume to differ. My remarks will refer particularly to the arguments that have been used in favour of increasing the duty on agricultural products.
The hon. member, for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), in his capacity as acting leader of the opposition, made a very able address setting forth what is undoubtedly the position taken by the Conservative party throughout Canada in regard to the tariff. It is evident that the pussy-footing attitude of the Winnipeg convention is to be departed from, and that they are now lined up under the banner of a higher protective tariff. Hon. members opposite are to be congratulated on that fact. They are also to be congratulated on the very able presentation made by the hon. member for 'South Wellington. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is to be congratulated on having a lieutenant who so ably performs the duties of that office when he finds it necessary to be absent from the house.
There were, however, expressions used and statements made which, I think, will bear some examination. The hon. member for South 78594-551
Wellington endorsed the statement that has been made so frequently that Canada is enjoying a season of unbounded prosperity. In a very large sense that is true judged by the tests that are usually applied-the test of bank clearings, carloadings, railway earnings, exports and imports. Undoubtedly Canada is enjoying a season of great prosperity. But then he went on to say that that prosperity was confined to the large cities, that it had not yet reached the small villages and towns and the rural sections. Again, in large measure, I agree with the hon. member for South Wellington. I had a conversation with a merchant in our local town just before coming east, and he made a remark to me something to this effect: "We talk about prosperity, but it has not yet reached us."
I admit that times are not as bad as they were six or seven years ago. The years immediately following the close of the war found the farmers of Canada in a desperate condition. The price of agricultural products had fallen to an alarming degree while prices in other lines had not come down, and during the first session that I was here I made a statement that was absolutely true, that I had to sell nineteen head of cattle and put aside $125 in addition to pay the wages for one hired man during the year. But though conditions are not as bad as they .were six or seven years ago, in a large measure it can be said that a condition still obtains particularly in regard to our major product- wheat-under which everyone who handles that commodity makes money out of it except the man who produces it. It is quite possible, Mr. Speaker, to produce an enormously large crop, a crop that is the main factor in the financial prosperity of Canada to-day, and yet produce it with little or no margin left for the producer after the expenses of production have been met. It is not the volume that counts; it is the margin of profit that remains for the producer. If to-day we were getting that twenty cents or twenty-five cents that we would like to get^that is, the twenty-five cents a bushel less that we are getting for wheat to-day as compared with a year ago-on the 400,000,000 bushels that have been produced, it would mean all the difference between comfort and distress on the farm. So I say, Mr. Speaker, it is not the volume that counts, it is the margin of profit. I can imagine that there were times of great prosperity before the civil war in the southern states, that prosperity was abounding, and yet the men who did the work got only their board and clothes out of it. There are many people throughout Canada to-day
86S
The Budget-Mr. Brown

who are contributing very largely to the great mass of production, who are scarcely getting their board and clothes out of it. There are those -who seem to think that the farmer is not entitled to a margin of profit, and if there appears the slightest indication that there is such a margin, they begin at once to move heaven and earth to find out how they can take it away from him. Just about a month ago I saw an article in the Montreal Gazette dealing with the question of the Crowsnest pass rates, and in that article this very sage remark was made, that if it had not been for the restoration of those rates the railway companies would be making so many million dollars more. We know, of course, that they would have made so many million dollars more, but those millions undoubtedly would have been taken out of the already depleted pockets of the wheat producers of the prairies.
Up to this point I have agreed fairly well with the hon. member for South Wellington, but here we must part company. We agree on the diagnosis of the disease but we do not agree on the remedy. The hon. member for South AVellington says that with one stroke of the pen all these economic evils can be corrected, and he proposes to use that pen to make increases in the tariff all along the line. And particularly has this been urged in regard to agricultural products. I am firmly convinced, Mr. Speaker, that increased protection on agricultural products cannot ultimately redound to the benefit of the producer. I oppose the increase for two reasons, first in regard to our major products on which we are still on an export basis. The mere putting on of a duty will not affect the price, for the price on the home market is always determined by the price on the export market. I oppose that policy because if the farmers of Canada should succumb to the temptation to seek higher duties on their own products we would immediately be met by demands from all other quarters for the .raising of the tariff on their products, and our last state would be worse than the first.
We are asked to look to the United States. Well, let us look. For over a century the farmers of the United States have been responding to the cry for higher and higher protection. They have followed in the trend of the protected manufacturer. What is the meaning of this cry for farm relief? No expression was heard more frequently during the last election in the United States than that demand for farm relief. I had hoped a year or two ago that the farmers of the United States had seen the folly of their position. I had hoped that they had seen that it was not possible in the final

analysis to protect them by means of tariff, and that they were seeking relief along other lines, by such bills as the McNary-Haugen bill. Not that I care to endorse that as economically sound, but I had hoped that they had found out that the farmers cannot be protected by tariffs. But it does seem that they have gone back to their old position and are now asking for higher tariffs on their products. It may injure us if these are granted, but it will be of no benefit to themselves, for the reason that their imports from Canada form an infinitesimal portion of their total production and consumption. The probability is that it will not affect their prices in the slightest degree.
I wish to direct my attention now to some of the articles that have been mentioned on which it is urged that higher duties should be placed. I shall not deal with the question of wheat. I do not think it requires any argument to convince hon. members that a duty on wheat would be of no value to the Canadian producer of wheat. We might make the duty five dollars a bushel and it would not affect our market price in the slightest degree. In a large measure, the same can be said of oats and barley. I want to come, however, to another of our products to which a great deal of attention has been directed. I refer to butter. It has been urged upon us that the dairy industry is suffering because of a large importation of butter. In my judgment, the dairy industry is one of the most prosperous industries in the country to-day. Protectionists make the mistake, whether deliberately or otherwise, of fixing their attention entirely upon one article, taking into account only one phase of the question; whereas we should look at the dairy industry in all its aspects and from a broad standpoint. As reported at page 792 of Hansard the hon. member for South Wellington -I think he was referring to last year'- said that we imported milk and milk products, exclusive of butter, amounting in value to $2,370,000. I do not think there was any intention to mislead as regards the figures, but I cannot understand where the hon. gentleman got those figures.

The great bulk of these imports comes from European countries and undoubtedly is made up of varieties of cheese that we do not produce in Canada, and therefore such cheese cannot in any real sense come into competition with our own product. I ask hon. members to keep that half million dollars in mind. Now let us turn to our exports of cheese. In the calendar year 1928 we exported to the value of $25,467,642. That is, on cheese alone we have an excess of exports over imports of $25,000,000. I turn to butter. According to this same schedule we imported $5,937,170 worth of butter, most of which of course came from New Zealand; but we also exported during the year $805,055 worth; that is, there is an excess of imports over exports of $5,132,115. But that does not tell the whole story of the dairy industry. We exported a number of other milk products in large quantities, for instance:

So the total excess of our exports of dairy products over our imports comes very close to thirty million dollars. Under such conditions as those it does not seem to me that the dairy industry is really declining. I have not been able to get the production figures of
butter for 1928, but I have the figures for

Then it is urged on every hand, and we believe it is true, that the home consumption of dairy products has very greatly increased during the last year or two. It is reasonable to suppose that that would be the case. We are told that the American tourist traffic means about $246,000,000 to Canada every year, and naturally dairy products would form a very large proportion of that total.

That is to say, for these six years, the proportion of exports to imports varied all the way from 20 to 1 to 60 to 1. Under such circumstances, will anyone seriously contend that an import duty, if it were raised to $4 a ton,

as advocated, following the United States, would be of any value to the Canadian farmer? And remember that when we export hay the average price is in the neighbourhood of 810 a ton, whereas when we import it the price is about 815 a ton. So that it would mean an additional tax of about 82 a ton upon hay.
Let me now refer to the question of hides and skins. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) quoted figures to show that we were importing $14,000,000 worth of hides, 810,000,000 being from the United States, while we were exporting about a similar amount; and he indicated something to the effect that these were simply cross entries and that we might wipe the whole thing off the slate and use our own hides instead of importing from the United States.
If the hon. member had taken more than a superficial view of the question he would not have assumed that position. It is true that we import hides to the value of $14,000,000 odd, from the United States SI 1,164,668, while we export to the United States $11,266,660 worth of this product. But there is this point to which I would call the attention of the house: That class of hides which forms the great bulk of our imports and exports consists of raw cattle skins, that is, the heavier hides. Now, on the hides we imported we paid a little more than 23 cents, and for the hides we exported we received 19 cents. Someone may say, "That is bad business; why export hides at 19 cents and import at 23 cents?" But a little close thought will surely convince anyone that there is a reason for this. The Canadian tanner is surely a business man . who can be trusted to buy what suits him, and therefore he pays that 23 cents for the class of hides he wants because he cannot get them in Canada. When I made a similar statement three years ago it was absolutely endorsed by Colonel Mullins, of Marquette, wh'o has bad a large experience in the cattle business and is faimiiloar wilth the fanning industry. He absolutely endorsed the statement that, the class of hides-or a-t least a large proportion of the hides-which the Canadian tanner requires cannot be obtained in Canada, so that he is obliged to go elsewhere for them. But we cannot consider this question of hides by itself; we must take into account the whole business of buying and selling hides and tanning them into leather, and also the selling of the leather. I notice that we sell to the United States such grades of leather as harness, sole leather, upper leather, with a very small quantity of other feathers, the total being $7,682,521. That is the country with which we cannot compete in these mat-

The Budget-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
ters. So that the total figures would indicate a situation something like this: Our excess of exports of hides and unmanufactured leather, so far as the United States are concerned, gives us a favourable balance-to use the term which is commonly employed-of something over $3,000,000; and taking our total exports into account we have a favourable balance of about $1,500,000. Now, if by one stroke of the pen a duty is imposed on hides, what do we do? We simply make it so much more difficult for the manufacturer, the tanner, to obtain his raw product, and we strike at this very profitable business which he is carrying on with the United States and other countries, securing no benefit for ourselves. The probability is that if we insisted on handicapping the manufacturer of leather in that way we should put him in the position where he would not be able to pay as good a price for that proportion of our own hides which he now uses.
I think I have shown that on some of our major products a protective tariff would not only do no good but would in some cases be actually harmful. If, however, it is decided that the people of Canada should not eat foreign produce, then I want to go the whole distance and not part of the distance. If we should not be eating fresh fruits and vegetables from the United States, then let us put on an absolute embargo. I do not propose to take the position which will make it. possible for those who live at the Chateau and at high class clubs, or in wealthy homes, to obtain these products, while the poorer people who are now using them in large quantities shall be deprived of the privilege. I wish to see us all on the same basis.
Now, Mr. Speaker, from the standpoint of the ordinary consumer I confess that there is not a very great deal in this budget; it does not contain much meat, of course, but we may be glad that it does not contain any poison. I am firmly convinced that the greatest danger to be faced by the Canadian producer to-day is that propaganda which will be carried on throughout the country to induce him to accept the principle of higher protection for his own products. I am sufficiently human to feel that if a man hits me I would like to hit him back; I am not defending that attitude but am simply making a confession, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said the other day. We can understand that attitude-

I heard it put this way the
other day, so it is not original with me: We
can understand a man, when he is struck on his right cheek, striking the other fellow on the left cheek; that may nolt be a very admirable disposition, but we can understand that feeling. Perhaps we can even understand the Christian doctrine, even though we do not practise it, that when a man strikes you on the right cheek you should also turn to him the left, but the one thing we cannot understand is the man who, being struck on his right cheek, strikes himself a blow on his left cheek. That is very similar to the Japanese revenging himself upon his enemy by committing suicide upon his enemy's doorstep.
It would be most regrettable, Mr. Speaker, if we should engage in anything of the nature of a tariff war, by rvhich we would hurt ourselves and do no one any good. It is generally conceded now that nobody wins in war; everyone loses. We may appear to win for a time, but ultimately everyone loses and that is equally true in a tariff war. As I have said already, the United States may hurt us with their tariffs but they cannot do themselves any good, and ultimately they will find that to be true; they may appear to enjoy some benefit when the tariff is first raised, but matters will readjust themselves in a short time and they will find themselves in the same relative position.
For the reasons I have indicated, Mr. Speaker, I feel compelled on this and on every other occasion to oppose the principle of increased tariffs on farm produce as a means of maintaining the prosperity of the farmer. Relief must be sought along other lines; we must seek it by reducing rather than by increasing the farmer's cost of production.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat was generous in his opening remarks in congratulating various hon. members of this house. I think one may very fittingly congratulate the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) in turn because, while one may find much with which to disagree in what he said, the hon. member has offered the first attempt at serious criticism to come from hon. gentlemen opposite, so far as I have heard, with regard to the speech, delivered by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) the other day, a speech which will be so long remembered by everyone who heard it. With the exception of the arguments presented by my hon. friend from Lisgar this afternoon the house has heard no serious attempt to deal with any of the propositions then advanced by the hon. member for South Wellington. It is quite

The Budget-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
true that we had the privilege, which we should have missed had we been deprived of it, of hearing once again from the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin); it is quite true thait we were regaled by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). in his own inimitable way, but until we heard from the hon. member for Lisgar this afternoon there had been, I repeat, no serious attempt to deal with, to meet or to criticize in any way those figures, facts and conclusions placed before the house the other day by the hon. member for South Wellington.
Instead of any serious attempt at argument we have been met with the reiteration of that platitude-for in reality it is only a platitude after all-which has been so widely broadcast throughout this country that we are enjoying a great and unexampled prosperity. This was the key note of the entire budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance this year; this was the key note which he emphasized last year, and one might say it was introduced as a counter-irritant, much as a dentist tells you that what he is about to do is not really going to hurt and that you must keep your mind fixed on something else. As I have said, the Minister of Finance stressed this prosperity as the key note of his budget speech last year. In presenting his budget, on February 16, 1928, he said:

Wb heard from the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) in the very able speech he made the other' day; we heard from the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher) only last evening, and we heard from the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) to-day as to the condition in which the farming community finds itself at present. But some wull say, "There is prosperity in the larger cities; your own people will tell you so and the leaders of finance and industry will assure you of it," tMr. C. W. Bell.]
It is because that has been so stressed; it is because it has been put forward as an excuse for all the deficiencies and wants of this budget, and the course pursued by the government, that I propose to address myself in the time at my disposal to a consideration of how far this alleged prosperity actually exists in those same large cities.
As an example, I will take the largest, richest city in the province of Ontario, the city of Toronto, and in order that I may not be accused of bias, I will refer to two great Liberal journals; to the two great pillars of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario- the Toronto Globe, pillar of cloud by day, and the Toronto Daily Star, pillar of fire by night. I will refer particularly to the pages of the Toronto Daily Star, that paper whose slogan is: Enterprise, efficiency and accuracy. We should expect authentic information from this paper, and in going hack to that period of which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) speaks I notice an article in that paper of August 30, 1927, at the time of the bountiful harvest of that year, which graphically describes the condition of thousands of wage-earners in the city of Toronto. The Star refers to the condition of one family, which it says is typical of many, and headlines the article thus:
Brave family to end of their resources
Child breaks down through malnutrition. Father out of work for a year.
The article continues:
They stuck to it through thick and thin until at last one of the children broke down under the strain. Malnutrition in reality, starvation, pure and unadulterated.
The article goes on to say that while some people were making money at that time this was the condition of over a thousand such families in Toronto, living in utter destitution, and who came through the last long winter no one knows bow and whose only outlook was to face another such experience. Such was the prosperity of thousands of city wage-earners under the Robb budget during the time of the bountiful harvest of 1927. Someone might say that 'that condition was only temporary, and to refute that argument I turn to the Toronto Star of December 7, 1927, which describes bow scores of wage-earners and workers were living in Toronto at that time. The Star speaks in particular of a deserted woman who was struggling to keep six little children alive, and to use its own words:
Here the deserted mother eked out an existence upon city allowance in one of a score of dens similarly inhabited and brushed by the pestilential blow of poverty.

The Budget-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
The article goes on:
The street was a mere tunnel through rotten houses. . . . shacks and dens where women live and children play-and die.
A pleasant picture of prosperity in Canada during the year of grace, 1927. Let us take the year 1928, when we had 'the greatest of all crops and the greatest possibility for national wealth, impeded as those chances were by some reasons which have already been given to the house. In the Toronto Star of August 10, 1928, we read of yet another typical, large city family. The article describes a man and wife with five children, the man left without a position through an illness of three weeks. He was without employment for one solid year although he had sought for any job that would keep body and soul together. But the level of employment was so high that he could not reach any of it, and so he went down and out. He had never learned how prosperous he was; he had never read the statements of the leaders of finance and industry. We shall hear presently from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) and he will probably tell us a great deal about seasonal employment. May I respectfully suggest that when the hon. minister approaches the house with his arguments on the question of seasonal employment, he will explain just what particular season would have been open to these unfortunate people when they sought work without return day after day, week after -week, month after month for years at a time.
Coming a little nearer to the present season, I read in the Toronto Globe of Wednesday, November 14, 1928, of a soldier who had served his country well but was forced to leave it. The article reads in part:
A decorated ex-aviator, artillery officer and British secret service operative, with high educational qualifications and impressive military recommendations, and with seven years, continuous service to his credit, is to be Canada's loss and the United States' gain as a result of his inability, in spite of two years' effort, to find suitable employment in the Dominion.
There were others who could not go; there were others who had to remain, and I see, by reference to the Toronto Star of December 18, 1928, how some of them were found at that time working their way around by singing and playing musical instruments in the streets. The article continues:
The men satisfied Chief Draper, through references from well known firms, that they were employed through no fault of their own. The chief sent for Captain Charles Nash, secretary of the Toronto and District Council of the Canadian Legion, who informed him that he could do'little toward finding work for the two and who added that dozens of members of tlie legion are unemployed.
"I feel it is a disgrace that men like these should have to stoop to what is only one stage removed from begging to provide for their families," the chief declared.
In the Toronto Globe of January 5, of this year the following article appears:
Long Bread Line For Midday Meal Yonge Street Mission Fed 350 Hungry Men *	Yesterday
Evidence of need and hunger has been manifest at the Yonge Street Mission during the past few weeks and Mr. Davis yesterday told the Globe that although the twice-weekly free meals are only beginning this week, from 100 to 150 lunches have been daily handed out to men who in many instances have been eager for even dried crusts of bread.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I come to March 2, 1929, the day after the Minister of Finance delivered his budget speech in the house. On page 4 of the Toronto Daily Star of that day the following streamer appears:
Hon. James Robb's Tax Reductions Reflect Canada's Prosperity
But on turning to page 2 of that same issue, I find the following heading over a photograph of a long line-up of destitute men on Yonge street:
Staff of Life for the Hungry
Underneath the photograph, we find the following:
Here is surprising confirmation of numberless hungry months and tight belts that stalk abroad within the limits of the city of Toronto during the cold, cheerless months of winter. These are the "rank and file" of the "legion of the unemployed". Yesterday 3.500 beef sandwiches and 100 gallons of coffee were distributed to the "wanting".
How that line-up of cold and hungry men must have felt a warming glow, if any of them possessed the two cents to purchase a paper, after reading about the Minister of Finance's tax reduction. Imagine a settlement worker entering one of those homes which the Star describes so graphically; he sees the condition of the shivering inhabitants of the "shack", as the Star calls it, and his heart is wrung with .pity. But he says to them, "We would like to do much for you but unfortunately the demands upon us from the thousands of unemployed in this city are so great that we are not able to do half of what we would like to do. We are short on clothes; we have not very much food to give you, but there is one thing I would like you to appreciate: Do you realize that the net debt reduction of the fiscal year of 1927-28 was $30,948,137.17?" The man looks up from his miserable pallet which, according to the Star, serves as his only bed, and a new light
874	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
comes into his eyes as he says: "What, Sir, is it really true? Was the actual net debt reduction for the fiscal year of 1927-28, $50,948,137.17?" The visitor replies: "Yes, my poor fellow, I do assure you that the actual net debt reduction for the fiscal year of 1927-28 was $50,948,137.17." "Then" comes the answer, "I starve in peace." How can we ever be sufficiently grateful for the real information, given us by these two great Liberal journals about the actual position of affairs in our large Canadian cities? Shall we not be full of gratitude to both these pillars of the Liberal party that makes us so aware of the full measure of our mercies and, particularly, to the Toronto Daily Star, that journal of enterprise, efficiency and accuracy? How far that little candle throws its beam across our prosperous province!
I notice that if we pass from the ranks of those who toil with their hands and come to another numerous class, we have those who are spoken of as the " white collar " workers, many of them in the employ of this government, such as postal clerks, letter carriers, civil service employees generally. How they must have thrilled to learn that the government shows a total revenue of $454,942,000; that the government proposes to pay out of surplus revenue the $60,000,000 loan maturing August first next, and to realize that meanwhile in the employ of the government are scores of married men with families who are working for the magnificent sum of $65 a month, or $20 a month less than the amount officially stated in the government's own publication to be requisite to purchase the bare necessities of life. If there is any greater reproach to be laid at the doors of any English-speaking government anywhere, I thank heaven I do not know of it.
Elsewhere in the budget we read that the estimated total expenditures are $385,160,000, out of which not one cent is to be expended on technical education, which doubtless takes its place beside old age pensions as an exemplification, in the eyes of the government, of a vicious principle.
But I started by saying that I too was anxious to congratulate where congratulations are possible, and I venture to extend my congratulations not only to the Minister of Finance but to other hon. gentlemen on that side of the house. For example, I desire to congratulate the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke). True it is that the results in his department show that last year was the leanest and poorest for many years in this country; but when we consider the blessed state of the workmen, as revealed by the Globe and the Star, and when we appreciate

what the Robb budgets have been doing for those men, let us congratulate the Minister of Immigration that there is any immigration at all.
I desire to congratulate my good friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) who was successful, either personally or by deputy, only about ten days ago in settling the strike of the textile workers in the city of Hamilton. What had caused that strike, by the way? It had been caused by the fact that the action of the government, following the budget of last year, had been such that the workers were compelled to take on much additional work, many longer hours, at the same pay which they had been receiving theretofore, or the works would have had to close down. They rebelled against that; they struck. The conditions were investigated. It was claimed that the manufacturer, a wolf in sheep's clothing, was trying to grind his men, but it was discovered upon investigation that the budget of 1928 had left those workers in such a position'that they would either have to accept added work, added hours, without any more pay, or go without a living at all. Therefore they went back to work and I congratulate the Minister of Labour upon that discovery.
I desire to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon a very recent conversion. About a year ago when the estimates were up in the house, I pleaded with him to have the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) permitted something more than the magnificent sum of $31,000 for widening and deepening the Burlington channel, a work which the Minister of Public Works agreed was absolutely necessary and the cost of which the engineers of his department had placed at $1,500,000. The Minister of Finance chided me severely for advancing the ridiculous proposition that more than $31,000 should be devoted to that work, but I see in the estimates which are brought down this year that there is to be allotted to that work one-third of the $1,500,000 which the engineers declared necessary. I congratulate the Minister of Finance upon- his conversion and I give him my honest assurance that I propose to watch very carefully the coming of the other $1,000,000 and to congratulate him when it comes along.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And then will the hon.
member vote for the government?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, because, unlike some hon. gentlemen, I preserve my principles whether I get anything or not. I congratulate, too, the government as a whole, although I did not agree with it in the least,

The Budget-Mr. Verville
because it succeeded in killing the proposition for the national highways. I congratulate the government on its success in that regard because, if that plan had ever gone through, it would have gone a long way towards revealing to all people, not only residents of this country but those who visit it from time to time, the true extent of the depletion that is going on in our forests and mines to the effect that United States workmen may be enriched and receive the wages that should go to the Canadian people.
Last, but by no means least, I venture to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), although he is not present at the moment. When I came to this house in 1926, on my first excursion into politics, I did not appreciate him. I had not the faintest conception of what the words " masterly inactivity " could ever mean. I had not the faintest conception of how a more homely phrase " safety first " could be put beside the words " masterly inactivity." But I know now. I have seen during the time that I have spent in Ottawa masterly inactivity brought to a pitch of perfection that I should never have believed possible. I have seen the right hon. gentleman with that grip upon office for which he has become so famous employ to the very, very best possible extent his policy of masterly inactivity which has lulled the Canadian people to sleep, which has made Canada the Rip-van-Winkle of the Rockies. The Prime Minister only a few days ago in this house sat opposite my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion), and when my hon. friend from Fort William made one of the most patriotic suggestions that this house has had the pleasure of listening to for many a day, and when in connection therewith he used the expression " red-blooded " the Prime Minister was only able to see amusement in it. Will the country care? Perhaps. Not long ago the right hon. the Prime Minister declared that he had discovered the necessity for a provincial conference in respect to the waterways question. Does anybody seriously believe for one moment that the Prime Minister sought in that conference anything but an evasion and a postponement of a decision on that question, a question that is pressing in this country at this hour? Do the people really care? May be. There are signs that there is somewhere an awakening actually beginning. There are signs that on the waterways problem, as on the power question, and in many other directions, the people at last are beginning to waken up to the fact that " do nothing " may be a good means of retaining office but it is very bad policy for the country.
We have had various opinions expressed in the course of this debate about the attitude which it would be proper and prudent for Canada to adopt if higher tariffs are enacted against us in the United States by the government of Mr. Hoover. But surely there can be no one found to say that the ideal behaviour for Canada, or the attitude for Canada to take would be to do nothing at all. And that has been the policy of this government under the Prime Minister. Mr. Speaker, if that is to continue to be the policy of this government, if the indifference of the people is to be counted on, relied upon, and exploited, then it cannot be long before the public will assert itself and will insist that others shall take the seats of those who now occupy the place of office in this land. Until then we have little to hope for, because the policy of " do nothing " has been so successful, from this government's point of view. But if the authorities in charge of the tariff proposals on the other side shall injuriously affect this country by the enactment of higher tariffs against us, we know of one party anyway that will insist that the only stand to be taken by this country shall be to say to our neighbours to the south, "We are most friendly to you, we want to be your friends now and always; we are willing to be conciliatory to every reasonable degree, but if our interests continue to be adversely affected then we will stand up for every one of our rights, positive, firm and unafraid. And, sir, if we cannot get that from the present incumbent of the Prime Minister's chair then it will be the duty of this country to assist us to go out and take it, in order that the interests of the country may be served, in order that its former high estate may be restored, and in order that those hopes that we have entertained for Canada- the hopes of our fathers and the hopes that have come down to us-shall once again stand a reasonable prospect of realization.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of speakers who have preceded me in this debate have taken a delight in praising the Divine Providence for the numerous favours with which it has overwhelmed the people of Canada under the present administration, especially during the last fiscal year. Some have even asserted-and it is my opinion- that we have a providential government, highly assisted by Providence above.
The hon. Minister of Finance, in introducing his budget on March the first last, apprised us that the finances of the country were in a healthy state, and that the period of surpluses is continuing in a most eneourag-
The Budget-Mr. VervUle

ing manner. This management of the public funds is of a nature, to my mind, to foster industry, trade, even agriculture, and to considerably increase in the minds of this people their confidence and trust in the future.
While heartily acknowledging the favours as stated in the budget speech, there are some for which, I think, we must thank both Providence and the government. I feel at liberty, sir, to make certain comments that in no way would I wish to be interpreted as reflecting on the present administration, but I deem it my duty to openly make them, trusting they may serve public interests and also those of the constituents that I have the honour of representing in this house.
The prosperity enjoyed by this country has been vaunted in every possible way. It is even stated that this prosperity is felt in every field of activity and throughout the Dominion. Like others I can see this prosperity, I acknowledge it and rejoice at it; nevertheless you will allow me to point out that the farmers, in certain parts of this country are not entirely wrong in complaining of the conditions prevalent at present, or rather are nearer the truth in complaining of their lot. By no means do I agree with the conclusions of the amendment, as set forth by the hon. acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie), when I express such views, because I think that this unfavourable situation of the farmers, in certain parts of the country, is due to certain causes or reasons, none of which can be imputed solely to the acts of the government. This unfavourable situation is brought about by numerous and various causes, some of which are traced to the farmers themselves-as it was so clearly pointed out on Thursday last by my hon. friend 1he member for Matane (Mr. Dionnel- others are traced to climatic or other conditions, and I am happy to acknowledge that the government is doing its utmost to help and encourage the farming class, yet I respectfully submit that it is in its power to do more. In certain sections of the country, our farmers have seen their work crowned with success. They received for their farm products top prices; however, I assert that, although this may be generally the case, there are nevertheless and very unfortunately-exceptions and that in certain sections of the country such are not the conditions prevailing.
I trust that no one will begrudge me the few minutes that I shall take to glance over Quebec. I may say, sir, that the farmers of certain parts of my province situated on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, where the county of Lotbiniere lies, have not been, this year, very fortunate as regards their crops and

are feeling the pinch of rather hard times. They are forced to seek elsewhere their seed grain and fertilzers of which they are absolutely in need; they are obliged to purchase those articles at top prices and must further pay excessive rates for freight. They are not so fortunate as the hon. Minister of Finance is in balancing his budget by surpluses; but like the governments which have preceded the present administration, they are in the sad plight of acknowledging at the end of each year, deficit after deficit.
Again, in no way do I wish to place the responsibility on the government's shoulders for this exceptional situation nor in any way blame them, but seeing that the budget brought down in the house, this year, informs us that the finances of the country are more than ample, I wish to take advantage of it by requesting the government to help, if possible, the farmers who might find themselves in the exceptional situation that I have just brought to your notice, and for which I request government assistance. I would therefore ask the government to grant the farmers which are in a precarious situation, what is granted elsewhere for other industries and in other sections of the country: a special rate, a reduction in freight rates for the shipment of goods of which these farmers are absolutely in need to maintain their land in good farming condition.
There is another feature to which I would like to draw the attention of the house: the budget makes no mention of changes in the income tax and I think on this score the government is worthy of praise. Unfortunately I cannot say as much with reference to the methods used in enforcing the Income tax act, especially in connection with our rural population, our farmers, the small land owners and the labourers of our countryside. These people with very few exceptions cannot pay this tax, simply because their revenue is only sufficient to keep their families in a decent manner. Nevertheless they are sent letters warning them that they have neglected to send in their statements, and must file same immediately if they do not wish to be dragged before the courts. These letters have attached to them a form which perhaps is quite the correct thing for accounting purposes but is a Chinese puzzle to those who receive them. These people are most of the time unable to fill in such forms; they are just as intelligent as city people or others, but this form is so complicated that they are unable to fill it in unless they can afford paying for a secretary or an accountant. This does not only apply to my riding but also to other sections. I do not

The Budget-Mr. Verville
wish, sir, to leave you under the Impression that no one, among our rural population, pays the Income tax; on the contrary; I am simply mentioning the fact that the forms as printed and sent to our people are too complicated. When parliament enaots a measure and puts it into force, why not use a simple method which our people can readily understand and willingly submit to? When such an act is surrounded with too much and difficult formalities, it is open to criticism by the ratepayers and they, by all possible means, try to avoid the law.. Let us place at the disposal of our people a simple form which the ratepayers will be able to fill in, they will then respectfully submit to the measures we enact.
With reference to the sales tax, I must say that the means applied in the enforcement of the act are entirely disgraceful, and let me, Sir, cite an example: here is small rural manufacturer who is sued for having neglected to make a statement of his sales during two months, and simply for the reason that during that period he had not worked his factory. Previous to that time, he had always sent in his statements monthly. During those two months he was not producing nor making sales, he therefore made no report; the man is sued without being given any preliminary notice and forced to pay considerable costs. I respectfully submli't, sir, that if a business firm, bank or any commercial institution adopted this method of suing its clients out of pure whim, without preliminary notice, I respectfully submit, sir, that these clients would be forced to close their doors, and this, under very short notice. Why should what exists in the business world not occur also in the intercourse between the government and the people? Why should the former not adopt the same methods?
These few comments are suggested to me by my sense of duty, not with a view to criticism but simply with the hope that the government, while endeavouring as in the past to improve the lot of our people, may give consideration to these few suggestions in order to alter somewhat the forms in use and thereby help our people as it is done in other business occupations.
I do not wish to close my remarks, sir, without performing a duty dear to me, that is to thank the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) for having been kind enough to extend some consideration to the province of Quebec in the distribution of railway lines. The county of Lotbiniere which I represent should have had 75 years ago a railway crossing it, which is so very necessary for the population of that county as a whole, but
especially for six or seven parishes on the south shore which are pressingly in need of such a railway.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) saying:
" Hear, hear! " His uncle, Dr. Rinfret, of Sainte-Croix, promised this railway to his constituents for 20 years, when he was member for the riding of Lotbiniere, relying, of course, on the promises made to him by the cabinet ministers of that day, promises like those which were made to me for some time past in connection with further extending the railway line.
I wish to thank the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) for the purchase he made, only I do not wish to be too enthusiastic in my thanks and praises fearing that, with the recollection of a promise 60 to 75 years old, I might be obliged to make another which might last a further 25 to 30 years.
A bill was introduced in the house on March the 1st last, and received its first and second reading. This measure enables the present government to purchase the Quebec, Montreal and Southern Railway. The hon. minister in introducing this bill, gave us the cost per mile for the construction which remains to be done. He informed us that there remained 20 miles to be built at an estimated cost of $40,000 per mile. Must we not infer from the figures he gave the house that he intends to do everything possible, as I surmise, to push this railway line through and locate the terminus at Quebec instead of Fortiervielle, in the county of Lotbiniere. He further added that this railway would serve to relieve the congestion of the Levis division, the third in importance on the Canadian National Railways which also contributed to the extent of $150,000 per year to the assets of the state railways. I assert that our national railway system will realize quite a profit, providing that they complete this railway just acquired-for its purchase is now a foregone conclusion

I was present in the railway committee room this morning, and the committee unanimously decided to adopt this bill, and I feel confident the government will sanction it.
I am here to look after the interests of my constituents, and I wish to draw the attention of the house to the fact that at present we are a a disadvanage as regards to railways. When I was praising, a few moments ago, the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), because he remembered the province of Quebec in the distribution of railway lines this
The Budget-Mr. Verville

year, I had also intended to place before the house certain statistics with which you are as familiar as I am; these statistics are very accurate, establishing the fact that we have not been unreasonable in our requests, moreover that we were absolutely within our rights in obtaining what was granted to us. The distribution of railways at present, in proportion to the population, is as follows: in the west the ratio is 1 mile to every 125 people; in Ontario 1 mile to every 250 people, and in Quebec, 1 mile to every 500 people. Our request was therefore not unreasonable, and if I have complimented the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), he deserved it, but he will prove himself more worthy of praise if he could double the railway lines of the province of Quebec, so as to establish the same proportion between the western lines and those of the east.
I truist, sir, that the period cf promises has come to an end, and that we are to live in the realm of realities so far as the railways we have been discussing are concerned. This line crosses the most beautiful part of my county, the oldest parishes on the south shore, pioneer parishes, not only of the county of Lotbiniere, but along the whole of the south shore, for it is from these places that sprung the population which settled all the south shore parishes; they are the most beautiful and prosperous in that part of the county and it is my opinion that the government by extending the railway just purchased will not only be helping a large population which is absolutely in need of this public service, but will considerably increase our national inheritance.
Before resuming my seat, sir, I wish to state that I am satisfied with the budget brought down, first, because it gives us surpluses; secondly, because it leads us to hope that the lot of our rural population will greatly improve inasmuch as the public funds will permit. I shall therefore cast my vote in favour of the budget and against the amendment moved by the hon. acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume that the debate on the budget having proceeded so far it is not now necessary to pay any further compliments to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), particularly as he is not in his place at the moment.
I have no present intention of discussing the fiscal questions involved in income, expenditure, surplus or debt reduction matters referred to in the budget speech of the Finance minister, but prefer to review the proposals of the minister for the most part as

they effect my constituents; or from the point of view of those of us here who represent the eastern counties of Nova Scotia, interested as we necessarily are in the coal and steel industries.
The minister stated that, as to the tariff board, the impartiality of the board had created a favourable impression among the Canadian people. May I say to the minister that the impression among the people of my native province is one of distrust as to the purpose for which it was created and contempt as to its accomplishments during the nearly three years of its apparently useless existence.
Another gem I quote from the budget speech:
In accordance with the traditional policy of assisting the development of our basic industries, the rates of duty on certain machinery and equipment used in the mining industry have been reduced.
Here is another:
There have been various references before the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation of interest to those engaged in the fishing industry and it is proposed to assist that industry further by placing certain articles on the free list.
Now let us see what the traditional policy of assistance to basic industry a la Hon. James Robb really means. In reply to these questions asked by me:
Coal Mining Machinery-Imports
Mr. Cantley:	.
1.	What was the value of all coal mining machinery other than stone dusting equipment imported into Nova Scotia during the calendar year 1927?
2.	What was the value of such machinery which was duty free?
3.	What was the value on which duty was paid?
4.	What was the total duty paid on such machinery?
5.	What was the value of all stone dusting equipment imported into Nova Scotia during the same period?
6.	What was the total duty paid on said stone dusting machinery?
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) on Thursday last-I quote from page 737 of Hansard-answered:
Mr. Euler:
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Imports of "Percussion coal cutters, coal augers and rotary coal drills and complete parts." entered for consumption in the province of Nova Scotia in the calender year 1927, amounted in value to $1,170, and the import duty collected was $234.
This is the only coal mining machinery and equipment which is separately classified for statistics, and the department has no record of the separate value of other machinery of this class imported or of the duties collected on such imports.

The Budget-Mr. Cantley
Therefore, it should seem that the traditional policy of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, so eloquently referred to will, perchance, assist the basic industry of coal mining by $234 yearly. Now I challenge the Minister of Finance to show from the records of the Department of National Revenue that the proposal I have read gives any greater relief to the coal mining industry than the figures I have just quoted as supplied by the minister of that department.
But, Mr. Speaker, the fishing industry was also to partake of the benefits of the traditional policy of assisting basic industries. The following articles are in part placed on the free list:
632c. Specially designed needles of a class or kind not made in Canada, for use only in repairing fish nets, when such nets are used exclusively for the fisheries, but not for use in repairing nets for sportsmen-Free, Free. Free.
682b. Metal swivels, of a class or kind not made in Canada, when used exclusively for the fisheries, not to include swivels for sportsmen's use-Free, Free, Free.
689b. Equipment, of a class or kind not made in Canada, and integral parts thereof, for distributing stone dust in mines-Free, 5 p.c., 10 P-c.
Stone dusting machinery, now used extensively in all our gassy coal mines to prevent coal dust explosions, which are extremely violent and disastrous in their effect, is still dutiable at 10 per cent in the general list.
Even among the friends of the government in their stronghold of the province of Quebec, no enthusiasm is shown for this budget. Let me instance that Liberal journal, the Montreal Daily Herald, where on page four, of its issue of March 4, the Monday following the budget speech of the Finance minister, I read:
A Colourless Budget
No one looking through the budget presented by the Hon. James A. Robb will doubt that Premier King was perfectly sincere when he told parliament a few days ago that the government does not contemplate holding a general election this year. It is true that when Mr. King made that statement he added that the government would of course reserve the right to call an election should unforeseen events make such a course advisable, but the possibility of such events occurring must be very remote in the view of the government, or they would never have brought down what is the most colourless and most disappointing budget which the present administration has yet submitted to the house.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I turn to the Nova Scotia press and quote from the Halifax Herald:
Mr. Robb yesterday opened the most colourless -and least satisfying-budget of his career as Minister of Finance. His speech told of gratifying Canadian progress and bounding federal revenues, but the public at large will find in the
tariff and taxation proposals of the present session little to promote more than passing attention.
So far as Nova Scotia is concerned, it is what the budget does not contain that will provoke comment and dissatisfaction. Proposals to aid the coal-steel industry, long delayed, have not materialized, at least, not in this budget.
Tariff changes are anything but "sensational".
There is nothing to offset the effect of the drawback item which remits the duty on bituminous coal imported for use in Canadian coking plants-an item which almost completely nullifies the provisions of The Domestic Fuel Act based upon a major recommendation of the Duncan commission. There is no inducement to use domestic coal in Canada coking plants with that drawback item in the tariff schedules. Either the item should have been removed or other provision made to counteract its serious and detrimental effect upon our own coal industry.
Similarly, there is nothing to offset the drawback of duty on bituminous coal imported for metallurgical purposes. Here again a direct recommendation of the Duncan commission is ignored.
The reduction of duty on certain types of mining machinery and equipment, welcome as they will be in proportion to their extent and value, form no adequate substitute for the direct recommendations of the Duncan commission which are entirely ignored. These reductions will help the coal industry a little, perhaps, and the steel industry not at all.
It may be that something will be done for the coal-steel industry before the house prorogues. It is earnestly to be hoped so. But the absence from the budget announcements of any mention of real aid is disappointing to the Nova Scotia people.
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that the latest Robb budget has really no tariff changes worth mentioning; knitting needles, brass swivels for fishing lines, eye dusting machinery, coeoanuts -goods never made or produced in Canada, of little importance in two of the major industries of Nova Scotia-fishing and mining; a gesture, only a gesture, small, cheap and of value comparative with its cost to the giver.
Next year the minister will, parad venture, make a gesture of assistance to our two basic industries-a matter which overshadows all other questions in eastern Nova Scotia. We have now waited two years, and another soon closes, without any suggestion of that relief recommended by the commission appointed by this government and which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) two years ago promised would be implemented practically in its entirety; which definite promise has not been honoured by the Prime Minister or by his Minister of Finance.
We apprehend .that, next session, in anticipation of an appeal to the country, some election bait will be 'thrown to us by way of long delayed coal and steel tariff readjustment. It will then be a case of "needis must when the Diel drives" and fully understood as such.
sso
The Budget-Mr. Cantley

That other ambassador of empire-.the honourable the Minister of Mines (Mr. Steiwart), built on generous and substantial dead weight lines, while on pleasure bent last summer was reported by the British press as having been right royally entertained in the great metropolis, when, after dining-let us assume wisely and well-he took occasion to advise the British coal masters to look alive and arrange to ship more of their coal to Montreal, where a great market awaited .them, or words to that effect. Such, Mr. Speaker, are some of the efforts of a minister of this government whose duty is to aid, foster, protect and extend the Canadian mining industry. Mention peat, and the minister is alert-ready bo spend forty, fifty, sixty thousand dollars in any year at that sink hole, the Alfred peat bog, into which we have already thrown $335,408.92, with no practical result worth mentioning or in prospect.
Canadians had recently the experience of seeing in action our lately created ambassador to Washington. What, Mr. Speaker, was his first diplomatic problem?-what the first great Canadian or international question to be discussed with our adequately protected friends of the United States? Simply this, Mr. Speaker, an abject appeal for charity; an appeal to the United States to allow some thousands of our Canadian citizens to enter that country and obtain from their manufacturers the employment denied them in their own country. Surely every Canadian worthy of the name was ashamed and felt humiliated by the thought that our country's accredited representative should approach our rich and powerful neighbour with so contemptible a request, and hang around the door of the Washington minister for a week or more reiterating his request that our people should be given an opportunity to work in American factories to produce, in many cases, goods which were afterwards exported to this country. Surely, Mr. Speaker, a national policy is needed, and a government that will provide it.
Now, we have the product of Soviet Russia pouring into the cities of Quebec and Ontario -coal mined under Soviet conditions of virtual serfdom in the Donetz basin, and sent here to buy food for their rationed miners who must work for a- dog biscuit bread ticket. This coal, on which the railway freight from the mines to the sea is absorbed by the so-called government of Russia, freighted six thousand odd miles through the sea of Azof, the Black sea, the Dardanelles, the whole length of the Mediterranean across the Atlantic to Portland, and thence nearly 250 miles

to Montreal, is then admitted duty free into Canada in competition with the labour of our Nova Scotians and Alberta miners. I would point out that the first cargo of this coal that came across the Atlantic was destined for and went to the port of New York. It was not allowed to be landed because the government imposed a duty of $3.42 per ton on it. The ship was turned around and sent up the St. Lawrence to Montreal, and there the cargo was discharged, and no duty paid.
A few days ago I asked the Minister of Mines a question regarding the quantity of Russian coal that had come in. He gave me some figures which I do not think are reliable, because my information is that the tonnage particularly the quantity which entered the port of Montreal is more indeed nearly 50 per cent greater than the figures he gave me. Be that as it may, the fact is that a large quantity of that coal has come into the country. The other day I saw a letter to a coal dealer from one of the prominent coal importers in Montreal, in which he pointed out that he was handling this coal and that he could assure the dealer that he would be in a position to supply it regularly throughout the entire coming season. Is this government to sit still; are all the resources of this government of no avail to deal with this matter? Canada is said to possess one-tenth of the total coal resources of the world, yet with many of our coal miners idle to-day our beneficent government allows coal to come into Canada from a Soviet-controlled country, transported over a distance of about 6,000 miles to enter into competition with Canadian coal, in direct disregard of all business economic principles. I appealed to the Minister of Mines, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Customs, and was told that the government is powerless. Each appeared quite unconcerned; they could not or they would not act.

speechtext:
No, I did not. I exempt the Minister of Finance from criticism; for he did exhibit some interest, some concern, and I think he will make some inqui^ into the facts. As for the others, they are hopeless.	. .
Now, Mr. Speaker, I point out that no tariff consideration is given the Canadian coal and steel industry. The excuse of the Minister of Finance for ignoring applications from other Canadian producers for adequate protection is the thread-bare assertion that they are still being considered by the tariff

The Budget-Mr. Canlley
advisory board. So far as the coal and steel industry is concerned, he is so contemptuous of it and of those interested in it that he does not even trouble to make this paltry excuse. One remark he does make, doubtless intended for the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) or those few who hold similar opinions; he says that the policy of this administration is not a high tariff policy but a low tariff policy; its policy is to eucourage production at home and the marketir g of our excessive production abroad. We see how a low tariff policy, with respect to iron and steel, not only encourages but has actually ensured the marketing in Canada last year of about $300,000,000 worth of American iron and steel, at least 75 per cent of which could and should be made in this country with enormous economic advantage to the steel and coal industry, the transport workers and other associated spheres of activity. During recent years the government, when giving consideration to the tariff, have paid no attention whatever to the interests of the Canadian coal miners or steel workers. The tariff tinkering of the past few years has clearly demonstrated that the tariff advisory board is an effective obstacle to any upward readjustment of the tariff, while the minister holds himself quite free to decree, and does decree, a downward revision of the tariff on his own initiative or perhaps at the solicitation of party friends. We had an instance of this last year in the boast of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he boasted that he had induced the minister to reduce the duty on coal for the sake of some of his friends, who, he admitted, had not asked for the favour.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, there is no sign from this government of any intention to comply with the recommendations of the Duncan report with respect to the coal and steel industry. The budget recently presented by the Minister of Finance does not even make a pretence to protect this industry and, so far as tariff relief is concerned, those interested either by way of occupation or investment may take what comfort they can from the knowledge that the present ministry have definitely turned a deaf ear to all their representations and requests for safeguarding protection or relief. The subvention of 50 cents per ton on native coal used in the Nova Scotia steel industry is ignored by the government and is still denied us, in spite of the findings made nearly three years ago by a royal commisison created by this government and notwithstanding the fact that three sessions of this parliament have been held since the commission completed its work on 78594-56
maritime claims. Not only have these remedial recommendations made by the royal commission been entirely ignored, but other recommendations are also treated as scraps of paper.
Just here I would like to refer for a moment to the coke oven bonus introduced by the Minister of Mines in April, 1927. I pointed out then to the minister that his proposal would be of absolutely no value to the Nova Scotia industry, and now I want to point out to the Minister of Finance and to the house that although that policy has been in force for two years not one dollar has been expended or claimed by way of bonus on Canadian coal used in the coke ovens of this country. The only report made so far is one as to about 15,000 tons used in Halifax in a small plant which was built to replace an antiquated city gas installation built some fifty years ago. Some of the friends of the government had under consideration, at the time this bill was passed, the location of coke ovens for the production of coke and gas in Montreal. They knew the provisions of the proposed act before the act was voted on, and before the plant location was decided on, and I want to point out to the house that they deliberately built their ovens alongside the Lachine canal. Why did they do that? They decided upon that location because they had no intention of using a ton of Nova Scotia or other Canadian coal in that enterprise. If they had so intended they would have located their plant down at the lower end of Montreal harbour, where Nova Scotia coal could have been unloaded direct into their storage bins fy-om the colliers. They decided upon their present location in order that American coal could be transferred direct from the holds of the steamers to the bins of the plant, and that is being done, therefore if they now for any reason should wish to take advantage of the bonus as to Canadian coal they would have to tranship the coal into lighters or by rail at a cost of from 50 cents to one dollar per ton, in order to get it to their plant, this due to its location. They knew what the proposals of the government would be and they simply ignored them. I do not know whether or not the government really knew how little value these proposals had; my impression is they did not care; they constituted a gesture. At all events the Minister of Mines gave us a gold brick, to use ordinary parlance.
I am sorry the Prime Minister is not in his seat; I should now like to put a few plain questions to him. I ask the Prime Minister if he is determined to continue to dishonour the findings of his own royal commission,



The Budget-Mr. Cemtley

the recommendations of which he said on August 30, 1926, speaking at Windsor, Nova Scotia, would have great weight in parliament. What did he mean when, from his place in this house on March 18, 1927, he stated:
The government hopes that by accepting as we have the recommendations of the royal commission on maritime claims virtually in their entirety, parliament and the country will recognize in the attitude of the government a wish to remove this great question as largely as possible from the arena of sectional discord and party strife.
Does the government's inaction and failure to implement an important portion of the Prime Minister's promise mean that his cabinet is divided on the question and that he is delaying and denying justice to Nova Scotia rather than grapple man-fashion with the reactionaries within the cabinet? Whatever the causes may be, the failure of the government to carry out the promise of the Prime Minister is producing an effect on the steel and coal situation in my native province and developing a state of feeling among those dependent on these two basic industries which bodes no good to the government and has checked and arrested plans of reorganization, extension and betterment of the industry, and we in this house, representing the counties primarily interested in and, to a very great extent, absolutely dependent upon the prosperity of these industries, demand a declaration of the policy of the government in regard to the carrying out of the recommendations of the Duncan commission in the matter of these two outstanding major industries of Nova Scotia.
Mr. Speaker, I take it that each member of this house is the representative of the electors of his constituency .and, as such, should by right support in the debates of the house those principles and ideas clearly expressed by the majority of those who sent them here. In my case, I have no shadow of doubt as to the views and wishes of my constituents on the matter of the implementing of those recommendations of the Duncan commission not yet acted on by the government. May I remind the house that less than a year ago, or to be exact on May 22nd last the Finance minister, in a moment of irritation characterized the expressions of dissatisfaction of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) and myself, as " whining." Again, during the debate of some few days ago, namely, on February 26 last, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), twice in one speech referred to what he called " continual harping " on the questions raised by the Duncan report and later in the same 
speech referred to what he called the " doleful wails " which come from time to time from those on this side of the house representing the province of Nova Scotia. These wholly uncalled for and most offensive gibes we hurl back at the authors of them, in entire justification of our attitude and discontent as to the measure in which the Duncan commission's recommendations have been implemented. I want to tell my worthy friends that so long as the rights of the province of Nova Scotia as I see them remain unredressed and so long as I can obtain sufficient oatmeal to supply my internal combustion engine, I will offer protests in this house on every fitting opportunity.
I now draw the attention of the house and the Prime Minister to some features of the Nova Scotia case and point out that a certified copy of a report of the committee of the Privy Council on April 17, 1926, to be found on page 6 of the report of the royal commission on maritime claims, reads as follows:
The Prime Minister is also advised that on the 12th day of March, 1926, the Premier of the province of Nova Scotia presented to the legislative assembly a resolution to the effect that his government is engaged in preparing a memorandum setting forth in detail the claims of that province with the object in view of seeking such adequate redress as will insure a return of contentment and prosperity to the people of that province.
The report continues:
The Prime Minister observes that it is most undesirable that any section of the people of the maritime provinces should entertain the opinion that their interests are being knowingly prejudiced, and that the public interest requires that every occasion for the existence of a feeling of grievance should, if possible, be removed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of the foregoing-declaration of the Prime Minister that the public interests require that every occasion for the existence of a feeling of grievance should, if possible, be removed, it surely was incumbent upon the Prime Minister to make every possible effort to that end notwithstanding which the undeniable fact is that no action has been taken by his government on two of the most important recommendations of the Duncan commission-recommendations accepted by him. I refer to their evasion of and deliberate refusal to implement the recommendation of the commission as to the two basic products of the maritime provinces which, he admitted, lie at the very foundation of the economic prosperity of those provinces. The Prime Minister, speaking in this chamber on the subject of the Duncan commission report on maritime claims on March 18th, 1927, said:

The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers
With reference to the natural basic products of the maritime provinces, namely, agriculture, fish, timber and coal, the government shares the view expressed by the commission that aspects that arise from the character of these natural basic products of the maritime provinces "lie at the very foundation of the economic prosperity of these provinces," and that, as respects these subject matters, "no greater dis-service could be done than to evade deliberate decision."
With regard to the question of coking plants, the commission's recommendation that immediate practical steps be taken, has been accepted and a bill will be introduced at the present session of parliament respecting the establishment of coking plants at convenient centres in Canada under government assistance, along lines approved by the special committee of the House of Commons, which dealt with the fuel question last year.
I submit that nothing more farcical has ever been put upon the statute books of Canada than the legislation arising out of that promise of the Prime Minister. Hundreds of coke ovens have been built and not one dollar has been paid by way of bounty, nor will it be. The Prime Minister continues:
The recommendation of the commission that the tariff advisory board should be asked to give immediate consideration to the customs tariff in its relation to coal, anthracite and coke, has been met. The matter is now before the tariff advisory board.
How long will it be there?

speechtext:
If the board lasts so long, but I submit such will not be the case, due to an impending change of government. The Prime Minister continued:
The question of protection on the primary products of iron and steel was, as stated in the report, under the consideration of the tariff advisory board at the time of the commission's investigation. Owing to the existing uncertainty of conditions surrounding the iron and steel industry in the maritimes, the government does not feel in a position to make at present any pronouncement with respect to the commission's recommendation of a renewal of the system of granting bounties with respect to steel when Canadian coal is used in its manufacture.
I submit that if the industry was in such bad shape surely that was the time when the government should have exhibited some interest and come to its assistance. In conclusion he says:
In concluding this statement, may I say that the government hopes that, by accepting as we have, the recommendations of the royal commission on maritime claims, virtually in their entirety, parliament and the country will recognize in the attitude of the government a wish to remove this great question as largely as possible from the arena of sectional discord and party strife, and a desire to give to our Dominion in the sixtieth anniversary of its founding, a renewed expression of the spirit V8594-S6J
which animated the fathers of confederation in their efforts to construct out of British North America a federal union under a system of government devised "to protect the diversified interests of the several provinces and secure efficiency, harmony and permanency in the working of the union."
God save the king!
Mr. Speaker, two full years have passed since the Prime Minister made these important declarations as to the policy of the government as regards matters which, he then rightly stated, lie at the very foundation of the economic prosperity of the maritime provinces. Two years have passed-two years of, for the most part, trial and stress for coal and steel-the two basic industries of Nova Scotia-as to which the Prime Minister stated no greater dis-service could be rendered than to evade deliberate decision thereon.
Now. Mr. Speaker, I charge the Prime Minister, his Minister of Finance, and the government with evasion of-to use his own words- "deliberate decision" on the vital matter of protection of these two natural, basic products of my native province.
